# Weekly earnings of employees

In this exercise, you will recreate ONS labour market analysis reported in the table [EARN04: Gross weekly earnings of full-time employees \[last accessed 21/02/2025\]](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/datasets/grossweeklyearningsoffulltimeemployeesearn04). Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using data from the Quarterly Labour Force Survey.

Learning outcomes:

-   To understand better how ONS earnings statistics are produced
-   To become more familiar with key variables from the QLFS
-   To learn  using  income weights appropriately

## Data

The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.

To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: [Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024](http://doi.org/10.5255/UKDA-SN-9349-3).

## Get set up

We will assume that the working directory for this exercise where syntax files and other materials  will be located will be a folder named `LFS_exercises`.   Once you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible inside `LFS_exercises`, for example in  another folder named `Data`. 

We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let's load the packages that are are going to need:

```{r}
library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data
```

Let's open the dataset.

```{r open, eval=c(-2,-5)}
#| echo: -1
lfs_od24 <- read_dta("~/Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta") 
setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")

### Importing a Stata format dataset 
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
            "Data/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    ) 
```

As there are many variables in the dataset, let's create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to  convert categorical variables  into factors in order to make them easier to understand and manipulate. For greater output clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using `droplevels()`.

```{r mydata}
dataex2 <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX) |> 
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05,ILODEFR,FTPT,SEX),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()
```


## Let's examine the dataset

We can use again `head()` or `View()` in order to inspect the data and the new variables:

```{r inspect}
head(dataex2)

View(dataex2)
```

## Examine weekly earnings

We can also examine descriptive statistics for weekly earnings

```{r desc1}
summary(dataex2$GRSSWK)
```
Non responses are coded using negative values, which may potentially impact on the outcome of statistical analysis. Let's retain  respondents who provided a valid answer only: 

```{r desc2}
summary(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0])
```

We could also have a look at weekly earnings using a histogram. Given that income data tends to be skewed to the right (a relatively small number of respondents have very large earnings), which may affect the legibility of histograms, we will restrict the plot to the earnings of 99% of respondents, leaving out the 1% highest earners. In order to find out about the relevant earnings threshold, we can type the command as follows:

```{r quantil}
quantile(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0],.99)
```

We now know that 99% of earners earn `{r} paste0("£", prettyNum(round(quantile(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0],.99)), big.mark=","))` per week. 



```{r plot}
hist(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0 & dataex2$GRSSWK<2499],
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles",                                           ### x axis label
     main="Gross weekly earnings in the UK, October-December 2024", ### Plot title
     freq=F)                                                        ### Displays probabilities rather than frequencies
```

::: panel-tabset
## Question

Plot the distribution of hourly earnings  up to the 99th percentile.

## Answer
```{r hourly}
quantile(dataex2$HOURPAY[dataex2$HOURPAY>0],.99)


hist(dataex2$HOURPAY[dataex2$HOURPAY>0 & dataex2$HOURPAY<68.8],
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles",                                                main="Net hourly earnings in the UK, October-December 2024", 
     freq=F)                                                       
```

## Examine full-time employees

It is important to remain mindful of definitions:

- *Employees* refers to people who whose jobs implies working under an employment contract for an employer; 
- *Employed* refers to people who are  both employees and self employed ie who have a paid job.

- Full-time or part-time refer to people's self declared working-time status, irrespective of whether they are employed or self-employed

LFS  data provides the INECAC05 variable, which records all nuances of economic activity (there are 35 of them!), including employment and self-employment. There is also ILODEFR which records the broad economic activity status (ie Whether employed, unemployed, etc.) and group together self-employed and employees.

We will now examine these  variables.

```{r sumboth}         
dataex2 |> select(FTPT,INECAC05) |> 
           summary()
```

If we further want to know about about the number of employees by working-time status, we will need to explictly restrict the analysis to those: 

```{r}         
ft.emp<-dataex2 |> filter(INECAC05=="[1] Employee") |>
                   select(FTPT) |> 
                   table()
ft.emp
```

There are `{r} paste0(prettyNum(ft.emp[[3]], big.mark=","))` full-time employees in the  sample.

::: panel-tabset
## Question

1. Provide a similar  description for summarised economic activity variable.
2. How many  *self-employed* respondents working full-time are there in the sample?

## Answer
1. 
```{r subset}
dataex2 |> select(ILODEFR) |> 
           table()
```

2. 
```{r}         
ft.emp.2<-dataex2 |> filter(INECAC05=="[2] Self-employed") |>
                   select(FTPT) |> 
                   table()

ft.emp.2
```


There are `{r} prettyNum(ft.emp.2[[3]], big.mark=",")` respondents in employment in the sample.
:::


## ONS estimates for employees' gross weekly earnings

The code below recreates the ONS results showing the distribution of income for full-time employees overall and by gender. 
It does it in three stages:

- First, we create a variable to flag the group of people we are interested in. 

   It may be a good idea to double check the definition used by the ONS [in its publication.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/datasets/grossweeklyearningsoffulltimeemployeesearn04) Looking at the notes under the Table EARN04, we learn that ONS figures are only computed for  respondents' main job, and also that *those earnings more than £100 per hour* are excluded. 


```{r ftEmp}

dataex2<-dataex2 |> 
             mutate(
                  ftEmp=ifelse(
                         FTPT=="[3] New Deal-FT" | FTPT=="[1] Full time" & 
                         HOURPAY<=100 &
                         INECAC05=="[1] Employee",
                         "Full-time employee", 
                         "Anything else"
                               ),
                  ftEmp=as.factor(ftEmp)
                   )
                  
table(dataex2$ftEmp)
```

- We then create a version of the data that takes the income weights into account:

```{r svy}
de.s<-   dataex2|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24)
```

... And finally, we compute  the results:

```{r med}
medinc<- de.s |> group_by(ftEmp)  |> 
        summarise(Median=survey_old_median(GRSSWK,vartype="ci")) |>
        ungroup()
medinc
```

The median weekly earnings of  full-time employees in the UK in October-December 2024 was £`{r} round(medinc[[2]][2])`. We need to keep in mind that by using the income weights, those with missing values on GRSSWK are automatically left out. This means that if we are not using these, we will have to exclude them explicitly (`GRSSWK>0`)

::: panel-tabset
## Questions

1.  What are the median weekly earnings for men and women in the UK?

2.  What are earnings at the lowest decile for males and females  in the UK?

3. Why are we using a different weight from exercise 1?


## Answers

1.  

```{r answer1}
mwesex<- de.s |> group_by(SEX,ftEmp)  |> 
                 summarise(Median=survey_old_median(GRSSWK,vartype="ci")) |>
                 ungroup()
mwesex
```
Median weekly earnings of women and men in the UK are respectively £`{r} round(mwesex[[3]][4])` and £`{r} round(mwesex[[3]][2]) `

2.  

```{r answer2}
dec1<-de.s |> group_by(SEX, ftEmp)  |> 
              summarise("Median"=survey_old_quantile(GRSSWK,vartype="ci",.10)) |>
              ungroup()
dec1
```
The median weekly earnings for men and women in the lowest decile in the UK are  respectively £`{r} round(dec1[[3]][4])` and £`{r} round(dec1[[3]][2]) `


3. Because earnings are computed for a specific subpopulation: those in employment with valid earnings data.

:::

## How many people working full-time are there?
This question relies on  a slightly different definition of full-time employment since this time we will be including the self-employed. This means we need to recreate a new variable to flag this group, or pass directly the definition to the estimation function. The figures published by the ONS can be found [here](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/datasets/fulltimeparttimeandtemporaryworkersnotseasonallyadjustedemp01nsa).

Let's follow the same steps as before: 

1. Let's flag full-time employees:

```{r ftEmp2}
dataex2<-dataex2 |> 
             mutate(
                  ftEmp2=ifelse(
                         (FTPT=="[3] New Deal-FT" | FTPT=="[1] Full time") & 
                         ILODEFR=="[1] In employment",
                         "People working full-time", 
                         "Anything else"
                               ),
                  ftEmp=as.factor(ftEmp2)
                   )
```

Let's the recreate our copy of the data that includes weights: 

```{r svy2}

de.s<-   dataex2|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24)
```
And finally, let's produce our estimates: 

```{r ftest}
fte<-de.s |> group_by(ftEmp2) |>
        summarise(survey_total(vartype="ci"))

fte
```

```{r corr}
#| echo: false
de.sa<-   dataex2|> as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)
corr<-de.sa |> group_by(ftEmp2) |> summarise(survey_total(vartype="ci"))
```

::: panel-tabset
## Question

1. The ONS table gives the estimated number of full-time employees as `{r} prettyNum(corr[[2]][2],big.mark = ",")`. Above, we get `{r} prettyNum(fte[[2]][2],big.mark = ",")`. Why is there a difference?

2. What steps above need to be different to get the correct estimate of the number of full-time employees?

3. What is the correct estimated number of: full-time employees, female and male full-time employees in the UK?

## Answer
1. Because we have used the wrong weights ie PIWT24, the weights that can only be used for earnings estimation

2. We need to create another version of the data with the correct weight: PWT24

```{r sa}
de.sa<-   dataex2|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

de.sa |> group_by(ftEmp2) |>
        summarise(survey_total(vartype="ci"))

```
3. 

```{r corr2}
### Full-time employees
fte2<- de.sa |> group_by(ftEmp2) |> 
                summarise(
                  survey_total(vartype="ci")
                         )

### Full-time employees by gender
fte.g<-de.sa |> group_by(SEX,ftEmp2) |> 
                summarise(
                  survey_total(vartype="ci")
                        )
```
In October - December 2024, there were respectively  `{r} prettyNum(fte.g[[3]][4],big.mark = ",")`  and `{r} prettyNum(fte.g[[3]][2],big.mark = ",")` male and female full-time employees.
:::
